title: The lion and the hare
hook: a small hare outwits a lion with patience and wit (Masnavi 1)
tomorrow: where would you go to say goodbye to Rumi?

segments.voice: Yesterday, the chickpea in the pot, boiled to make it good, not out of hate: cooked, not punished. Today, a face in the water.
screen: `COOKED, NOT PUNISHED.` → `A FACE IN THE WATER.`

segments.voice: Lean over a still pond, or a dark phone screen, and a face looks back at you before you're ready for it. Rumi built a whole story in the Masnavi around that moment. A lion terrorizes the animals of a valley. To stop the hunting, they strike a deal: every day, one of them will go to him on its own. Then it's the hare's turn. A lion, a hare, and a well. How does the small one win?
screen: `A FACE IN THE DARK SCREEN.` → `ONE ANIMAL A DAY.` → `THEN, THE HARE'S TURN.`

segments.voice: The hare takes its time. It arrives late, on purpose, and the lion is roaring with hunger and rage. The hare bows: forgive me. I set out with a companion, but another lion stopped us on the road and took my friend. He says this valley is his. The lion is furious. Show me this rival. The hare leads him to a deep well and steps back, trembling: he's down there. The lion leans over the edge and looks into the water, and there is a lion, glaring up at him, with a hare beside it. He leaps at it, and the well takes him. The small one wins with patience and wit, not weight. A version also sits in Kalila wa Dimna, a book of animal fables. Rumi turns it inward, and that's the part to feel. The rival in the well was the lion's own face. Rumi says, paraphrased: many a fault you see in others is your own nature, showing in them. The lion attacked his reflection and drowned in it. So the hare's victory has two lessons. Outside: weight isn't everything; a calm, clever mind can undo brute force. Inside: before you leap at the face glaring up at you, check whose face it is. Wit over weight.
screen: `THE HARE ARRIVES LATE, ON PURPOSE.` · `ANOTHER LION, IN THE WELL.` · `THE LION LEAPS AT HIMSELF.` · `YOUR FAULT, SHOWING IN THEM.` · then, large: `WIT OVER WEIGHT.`

segments.voice: Fill a glass or bowl with water, or turn your phone screen dark, and look into it until your face settles there. Hold your gaze softly for the sit. When an irritation with someone comes to mind, ask the face in the water, gently, whether some of it is yours.
The lion and the hare: Rumi's fable of a small hare that beats a lion with patience and wit, and a lion who leaps at his own reflection.
screen: `THE LION AND THE HARE — today's word`.

segments.voice: Pocket this before the next showdown: wit over weight, and check the face in the well first. Seven of Rumi's eight.

howItsDone: Sufi teachers use the lion and the hare both as a fable of wit over force and as a mirror: the faults we attack in others may be our own, reflected.
